title: SharePoint vs Confluence vs Google Drive: India Guide

html:
The Short Answer (Then We’ll Get Into the Mess)

For most Indian enterprises already on Microsoft 365, SharePoint wins. Not because it’s perfect, but because the integration depth, compliance tooling under Microsoft Purview, and DPDP (Digital Personal Data Protection) Act alignment make it the least-risky bet at scale. “Most” is doing a lot of work in that sentence, though, and the exceptions are real enough to matter.

We’ve spent close to two decades helping Indian businesses move off on-premise servers, outdated intranets, and whatever file-sharing frankenstein they cobbled together back in 2011. So this isn’t theoretical. It comes from watching a Bengaluru logistics firm lose three months of migration work because they picked Confluence for document management without realising how painful external sharing governance gets past 500 users. And from watching a Hyderabad pharma distributor nearly go with Google Drive before we walked them through what DPDP data residency requirements would actually mean for their GCP region choices. Those aren’t cautionary tales deployed for effect. They just happened.

Let’s be direct about each platform before we get to the table.

What Each Platform Actually Is (And What It Isn’t)

This matters because the marketing pages for all three make them sound more or less interchangeable. They aren’t.

SharePoint is Microsoft’s enterprise content management and intranet platform. Deeply woven into Microsoft 365. When your users are already living in Teams, Outlook, and OneDrive, SharePoint is essentially the document management and intranet layer sitting underneath all of it. Version control, metadata, permission inheritance, records management, site-level governance at scale. These aren’t checkbox features. They’re architectural decisions baked into how the platform works, and that distinction matters when things get complicated.

Confluence (by Atlassian) started as a wiki. It’s genuinely good for software development teams, technical documentation, and engineering knowledge bases, and it pairs cleanly with Jira. But it was never designed for enterprise document management. When you try to push it in that direction, you hit walls around external sharing, folder structures, and compliance auditing that its architecture simply wasn’t built for. That’s not a criticism of Atlassian. It’s just what the tool is and what it isn’t.

Google Drive via Google Workspace is a cloud storage and real-time collaboration tool. Honestly excellent for small teams that need speed. Shared drives, Docs, Sheets with simultaneous editing. Works beautifully for a 30-person startup. Scaling to 3,000 people with complex permissions, departmental access hierarchies, and audit trail requirements is a different problem entirely, and that’s where the seams start to show.

SharePoint vs Confluence: Where the Real Differences Show Up

Most Indian IT teams comparing sharepoint vs confluence are doing so because they’ve already got a mixed environment. Some teams on Jira and Confluence for dev work, the rest of the business on Microsoft 365. That’s the actual context. And in that context, the question is really about whether you standardise on one platform or keep running two in parallel.

Maintaining two is expensive. Not just in licensing costs either. Training, IT support overhead, and the constant low-grade confusion about which system holds the authoritative version of any given document. We’ve watched this fail repeatedly, especially in mid-size companies between 200 and 800 employees where the IT team is too small to enforce governance across two separate content platforms at once.

That said, pulling Confluence away from an engineering team that genuinely lives in it is a political fight you might not want to pick. What we typically recommend: keep Confluence for technical documentation and dev wikis, use SharePoint for everything else. HR policies, finance documents, sales collateral, executive communications, project delivery records. The critical piece is a written policy specifying which tool owns which content type. Without that, you get sprawl. Fast.

From a pure feature standpoint, SharePoint’s metadata and managed metadata term stores are substantially more capable than Confluence’s labelling system. For regulated industries like BFSI or pharma, where documents need lifecycle policies, retention labels, and audit logs, there’s really no comparison. Confluence simply wasn’t built for that use case, and no amount of configuration changes that.

SharePoint vs Google Drive: The Question Indian SMBs Ask Most

The sharepoint vs google drive conversation usually surfaces when a growing company is deciding between Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace as their primary productivity suite. That’s really the underlying choice. Once you pick the suite, the collaboration platform largely follows from it.

Google Drive’s pricing looks attractive upfront. Google Workspace Business Starter runs cheaper per seat than Microsoft 365 Business Standard. But total cost of ownership across three years, especially once you factor in third-party security tools that Indian enterprises often need to bolt onto Google Workspace for DLP (Data Loss Prevention) and eDiscovery, tends to close that gap considerably. Sometimes past it. Worth running the actual numbers rather than comparing sticker prices.

On the compliance side, Microsoft’s native tooling is ahead right now. Microsoft Purview covers eDiscovery, data classification, sensitivity labels, and audit logs within the same admin console you’re already using. Google has equivalent tools, but they’re more spread across different admin surfaces and third-party add-ons, which adds operational overhead.

For enterprises thinking about DPDP Act compliance, Microsoft has confirmed Azure data centres in India, Pune and Hyderabad regions, with explicit data residency controls. Microsoft 365 data residency for Indian tenants is configurable. Google Cloud also has Mumbai and Delhi regions, so this isn’t a clean Microsoft-only win. But Microsoft’s compliance documentation and legal framework around Indian data handling is more developed right now. That could shift. Today, though, this is where things stand.

The Decision Table: Side-by-Side for Indian Enterprise Buyers

Criteria SharePoint (Microsoft 365) Confluence (Atlassian) Google Drive (Workspace)
Best fit Enterprises, BFSI, regulated industries, M365 shops Software and engineering teams, Jira-first orgs SMBs, startups, Google-first teams
Document management depth Very high (metadata, versioning, records management) Limited (wiki-oriented, not document-first) Moderate (good for basics, limited governance)
Microsoft 365 integration Native Via connectors, not native Requires third-party bridging
DPDP Act / compliance tooling Strong (Purview, sensitivity labels, India data residency) Basic (relies on Atlassian Cloud security framework) Moderate (Google Workspace DLP, Vault)
Licensing cost (per user/month, approx.) Included in M365 Business Standard (~INR 715) Confluence Standard ~USD 5.75/user Workspace Business Starter ~USD 6/user
External sharing governance Granular (site-level, link expiry, guest access policies) Limited at enterprise scale Workable for small teams, harder to govern at scale
Migration tooling maturity Strong (SPMT, Mover, third-party tools) Atlassian migration assistants available Google Workspace Migration Tool available
Intranet capability Strong (SharePoint Communication Sites) Limited Not designed for intranets

Pricing figures are approximate as of Q1 2025. Actual enterprise pricing varies by volume and negotiated agreements. Verify current rates directly with vendors before budgeting.

When SharePoint Consulting Services Actually Make a Difference

Here’s the honest version: SharePoint is not a “turn it on and go” platform. Out of the box, it’s powerful. But without governance design, information architecture planning, and proper permission configuration, it becomes a shared drive with a fancier URL. We’ve inherited enough broken SharePoint environments to say this without hedging.

The situations where professional sharepoint consulting services save real money and time:

  • You’re migrating more than 1 TB of content from file servers, old SharePoint on-prem versions, or another platform entirely. Edge cases in large migrations are relentless: broken metadata, nested folders that blow past SharePoint’s 400-character URL limit, on-prem permissions that don’t map cleanly to modern SharePoint. These aren’t hypotheticals. They’re the first three things we look at on every migration scoping call.
  • Actual retention policies, sensitivity labels, legal hold capability, and audit trails that would hold up under regulatory review. Not “put documents somewhere.” A genuinely compliant document management system.
  • Your organisation has more than three departments with different access requirements and document types. Because information architecture decisions made in week one will either pay off for years or create a governance mess you’ll spend years trying to unwind. Not a lot of middle ground there.
  • You’re running a microsoft 365 migration services engagement where SharePoint is one piece of a larger move to the cloud, alongside Exchange Online, Teams, and potentially Dynamics 365. Coordinating those workloads without a real plan is how things go sideways, fast.

The companies that do worst with SharePoint are the ones who had IT set it up over a weekend with no content strategy. The ones that do best spent two weeks on governance design before moving a single file. That’s not consulting for its own sake. It’s just what the platform requires to actually work properly.

For sharepoint migration services specifically, the tooling has improved considerably. Microsoft’s SharePoint Migration Tool (SPMT) handles most file server and SharePoint on-prem migrations reasonably well. But it doesn’t think. It won’t flag that your folder structure will cause URL-length failures, or that your on-prem permission groups don’t have equivalents in Entra ID. That judgment layer is still a human job.

Real Migration Scenarios We’ve Seen in India

A manufacturing client in Coimbatore was running SharePoint Server 2013 on-prem. Classic setup: IT had full control, nothing in the cloud, everything on local hardware. The trigger to move was a hard drive failure that took down a production planning library for 36 hours. No cloud backup. After that, they were motivated. We scoped a phased migration to SharePoint Online, starting with the three highest-traffic document libraries. Total migration took about 14 weeks including governance setup. Not because the file transfer was slow, but because they had 11 years of accumulated folder chaos to rationalise first.

A Pune-based NBFC (Non-Banking Financial Company) came to us mid-way through a failed Confluence implementation. Their IT head had chosen Confluence based on a recommendation from the dev team, without realising the compliance officer’s requirements around document retention and audit trails weren’t achievable without significant custom development. They switched to SharePoint. The migration from Confluence to SharePoint Online took about six weeks. The bigger work was building the information architecture their compliance requirements actually demanded.

Both cases had material business consequences. Not platform preferences. Real operational risk tied to a platform decision made without the full picture.

FAQ

Is SharePoint better than Google Drive for Indian businesses dealing with DPDP compliance?

Generally yes, for larger organisations. Microsoft 365’s native compliance tooling (Purview, sensitivity labels, retention policies) is more integrated and better documented for regulated Indian industries like BFSI and healthcare. Google Workspace has improving compliance tools, but they require more configuration and often third-party additions. For a 20-person startup with no compliance obligations, this distinction barely matters. For a 500-person NBFC, it matters considerably.

Can we use both Confluence and SharePoint in the same organisation?

Yes, and many Indian enterprises do exactly that. The key is a clear content policy: Confluence owns technical and developer documentation, SharePoint owns everything else. Without that policy written down and actually enforced, both platforms fill up with the same content types and nobody knows which one to trust. We’ve seen this exact problem across multiple organisations. The tool split is workable. The undisciplined split is not.

When should we bring in sharepoint consulting help instead of doing it ourselves?

If you have fewer than 100 users, basic folder structures, and no compliance requirements, a capable internal IT person can set up SharePoint Online using Microsoft’s documentation. Once you’re past that threshold, whether that’s significant migration volumes, regulated content, complex permission structures, or integration with other Microsoft 365 workloads, the cost of getting it wrong almost always exceeds the cost of getting experienced help. We’re not saying that to sell services. We’re saying it because we’ve cleaned up enough self-managed migrations to know exactly where the failure points are.

The Honest Closing Take

If you’re an Indian enterprise already on Microsoft 365, there’s almost no scenario where Confluence or Google Drive wins for your primary collaboration and document management needs. SharePoint, set up properly, is the more governable, more compliant, and ultimately more scalable option. That phrase “set up properly” is carrying real weight there.

If you’re a dev-heavy organisation and your engineers genuinely live in Jira, keep Confluence for what it does well. Just don’t try to make it do enterprise document management. It will disappoint you, and you’ll end up migrating anyway.

And if you’re evaluating platforms right now for a migration or a greenfield Microsoft 365 deployment, get a sharepoint consulting engagement scoped before you lock in your information architecture. Not because SharePoint is hard, but because the decisions made in week one shape everything that follows. Fixing them later costs more than getting them right the first time. Every time.
